newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai grain storage strained by bumper crops.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai grain storage strained by bumper crops.

text.p: Grain storage facilities in China's biggest city, Shanghai, are holding more than 20 percent above capacity after the record grain harvest of 1996, a city agriculture official said on Monday.
Shanghai has the capacity to store three million tonnes of grain, the director of the Shanghai City Government Agriculture Commission, Fan Deguan, said.
"Grain production (in the past year) has been very high so there is 20 percent more than capacity held in the city's central reserves," Fan told a news conference.
He said the government had purchased more grain than usual from local peasants in the past year to help them get rid of their produce.
Under the government's price protection policy, the procurement price paid to peasants for their grain was two yuan, or 24 U.S. cents, a kg (2.2 lb), Fan said.
The retail price for grain in Shanghai is around 3.20 yuan per kg, sources in the city said.
Fan said Shanghai's total annual grain output had remained stable at 2.05 million tonnes for the past four years.
Output in 1997 would be about the same as available land area for grain production had not changed, Fan said.
Figures released last week by the Shanghai statistical bureau showed 1996 grain production in the city was 2.12 million tonnes, up 2.8 percent on the previous year.
The city's total agricultural output value for 1996 was 19.8 billion yuan, up 5.8 percent on the previous year and accounting for 2.6 percent of China's total, the figures show.
Grain demand in Shanghai, which Fan said has a population of 13 million, was six million tonnes a year, a figure that included food, feed and industrial use.
The shortfall between local production and demand was made up with imports from other parts of China and, especially for animal feed needs, from abroad, Fan said.
China had a record grain crop in 1996 of 480 million tonnes. Corn output has been officially estimated to reach 119 million tonnes, up from the 112 million tonnes of 1995.
